pages.title: Capital, panics and gold
pages.lede: Between 1895 and 1904 a wave of mergers swept American manufacturing, and the panics of 1893 and 1907 each cut real output by about a tenth. In 1896 William Jennings Bryan denounced the gold standard as a 'cross of gold'; McKinley signed the Gold Standard Act in 1900, and after the panic of 1907 spurred reform, Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act in 1913.
body: In the summary of the introduction to Naomi Lamoreaux's book, 'Between 1895 and 1904 a great wave of mergers swept through the manufacturing sector.' Most took the form of 'the simultaneous merger of many or all competitors in an industry into a single, giant enterprise', and New Jersey's 1888 'general incorporation law for holding companies' encouraged them. [[c-us5-fin-merger]] In the publisher's summary of her findings, most of the consolidations were less efficient than the new rivals that appeared almost immediately, and they quickly lost their dominance of their markets. [[c-us5-fin-lamoreaux]] U.S. Steel was created when Morgan's group bought Carnegie Steel in 1901 (US5.1). [[c-us5-ind-carnegie]]

In the panic of 1893 the Treasury's gold reserves, $190 million in 1890, fell to about $100 million, and 340 banks suspended operations between mid-July and mid-August. [[c-us5-fin-1893]] Unemployment estimates differ: the Federal Reserve History essay gives a peak of 17 to 19 percent, and a New York Fed account an estimated rate 'above 11 percent from 1894 to 1898.' [[c-us5-fin-unemp]] In February 1895 President Cleveland told Congress of an arrangement with private parties for gold 'slightly in excess of $65,000,000', at least half of it 'to be supplied from abroad.' [[c-us5-fin-cleveland]]

In Chicago on 9 July 1896 William Jennings Bryan closed his speech: 'You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns. You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.' [[c-us5-fin-bryan]] The image recalls the Passion; in Matthew 27:29, 'after twisting some thorns into a crown they put it on his head.' [[c-us5-fin-matt]] On the election of 1896 and the Populists, see US5.6. In 1900 McKinley signed the Gold Standard Act. [[c-us5-fin-goldact]] Was gold a mistake? Milton Friedman (1990) argued that the act of 1873 that dropped silver 'cast the die for a gold standard', at a cost, against the conventional view that it was 'a piece of good fortune'; François Velde (2002) calculated that, without it, bimetallism 'would have survived' for another twenty years, or until the First World War had India not abandoned silver, though the United States would still have seen a sharp inflation early in the twentieth century. Friedman treats the move to gold as avoidable; Velde's model suggests that the act brought it forward by about two decades. Neither source names a defender of the conventional view, but Michael Bordo and Hugh Rockoff (1996), writing of gold in general rather than the act of 1873, argue that in 1870-1914 adherence to gold 'was a signal of financial rectitude, a "good housekeeping seal of approval"' that eased access to European capital. [[c-us5-fin-friedman]]

In 1907 the suspension of the Knickerbocker Trust set off a new panic; J. P. Morgan 'changed his mind and quickly released aid', and the Clearing House banks also helped. The Federal Reserve History essay gives falls of 17 percent in industrial output and 12 percent in real GNP in 1908. [[c-us5-fin-1907]] MeasuringWorth's real GDP series shows a fall of 10.9 percent from 1907 to 1908, after one of 10.4 percent from 1892 to 1894. [[c-us5-fin-mwgdp]] The panic 'spurred the monetary reform movement', and on 23 December 1913 Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act, which provided for 'between eight and twelve' regional Reserve Banks. [[c-us5-fin-fedact]]

pages.title: Labor: wages, unions and strikes
pages.lede: Manufacturing workers' real earnings rose by about 37 percent between 1890 and 1914, and their working week fell from about 60 hours to about 51 by 1920. The Knights of Labor rose and collapsed in the 1880s, and the strikes at Homestead in 1892 and Pullman in 1894 ended in defeat, against the state National Guard at Homestead and a federal injunction and troops at Pullman. The Triangle fire of 1911 killed 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women.
body: The manufacturing workweek of the 1800s was, in Robert Whaples's words, 'very long by modern standards': 60.7 or 61.8 hours in 1880, depending on the report used, 59.6 in 1900 and 51.2 by 1920. [[c-us5-lab-hours]] Albert Rees found that 'the real earnings of manufacturing workers rose 37 per cent from 1890 to 1914', as average hourly money earnings rose from $0.144 to $0.220; his result depends on his cost-of-living index. [[c-us5-lab-rees]]

The Knights of Labor grew to 'over 700,000 members by October 1886'. They 'welcomed women and African Americans', but had 'a terrible record' toward Chinese Americans, and their membership 'quickly fell to 100,000 by 1890'. [[c-us5-lab-knights]] In 1886 Samuel Gompers became the first president of the new American Federation of Labor. [[c-us5-lab-gompers]] On 4 May 1886 a bomb at Haymarket, in Chicago, led to the deaths of seven police officers; eight anarchists were tried and four executed. The affair was 'used widely to discredit the Knights, although they took no part in it.' [[c-us5-lab-haymarket]] In The Making of American Exceptionalism (1993), Kim Voss argues that for most of the nineteenth century the American labor movement resembled its English and French counterparts, and that it took a different path only after the Knights of Labor collapsed. She rejects explanations that put American labor's weakness down to the nature of American society itself. [[c-us5-lab-voss]] On the other side, Seymour Martin Lipset and Gary Marks, in It Didn't Happen Here: Why Socialism Failed in the United States, address the question Werner Sombart posed in 1906, their reviewer Michael Biggs notes, and argue that four factors were decisive, among them the disadvantages the American political system posed for third parties and a culture of antistatism and individualism; Biggs places Voss among those who single out repression instead. [[c-us5-lab-lipset]]

At Homestead on 6 July 1892 about 300 Pinkerton guards hired by Henry Clay Frick fought striking steelworkers; at least three Pinkertons and seven workers were killed. 8,500 soldiers of the state National Guard were sent in, and by 21 November the union had given up. [[c-us5-lab-homestead]] In the Pullman boycott of 1894 the American Railway Union, 150,000 strong and led by Eugene V. Debs, refused to handle Pullman cars, and 'the boycott crippled rail traffic nationwide'. A federal injunction and federal troops defeated it, in violence that 'left dozens dead.' [[c-us5-lab-pullman]] In In re Debs (1895) the Supreme Court upheld the injunction: 'The strong arm of the national government may be put forth to brush away all obstructions'. [[c-us5-lab-debs]]

The 1900 census found more than 1.75 million children aged ten to fifteen at work. The National Child Labor Committee was founded in 1904, and Lewis Hine photographed for it; the Keating-Owen child labor act of 1916 was declared unconstitutional in 1918, in Hammer v. Dagenhart. [[c-us5-lab-child]] On 25 March 1911 the Triangle fire in New York killed 146 workers. 'Most of the dead were recent immigrant Jewish and Italian women between the ages of sixteen and 23', and workers 'jammed up at illegally locked exits'. Of the Factory Investigating Commission that followed, the Department of Labor writes that '13 of 17 bills it submitted became law.' [[c-us5-lab-triangle]]

pages.title: The new immigration
pages.lede: From 1892 to 1924 more than 12 million immigrants were processed at Ellis Island, and arrivals shifted toward southern and eastern Europe: in 1900-09 Austria-Hungary, Italy and Russia each sent more than 1.5 million people, Germany fewer than 330,000. Recent studies find that immigrants advanced at natives' pace and their children faster, while another finds that immigration also produced a political backlash. Congress excluded Chinese laborers in 1882 and imposed a literacy test, over President Wilson's veto, in 1917.
body: From 1892 to 1924 Ellis Island was 'America's largest and most active immigration station', and 'over 12 million immigrants were processed' there. [[c-us5-immig-ellis]] Where immigrants came from changed. By the Department of Homeland Security's count of people obtaining permanent residence, 1,445,181 came from Germany and 267,660 from Italy in the 1880s; in 1900-09, 2,001,376 came from Austria-Hungary, 1,930,475 from Italy and 1,501,301 from Russia, and only 328,722 from Germany. These are counts by country of last residence, not by nationality or religion, and Table 2 gives no separate figure for Poland in 1900-19. [[c-us5-immig-dhs]] On the mass migrations of these decades worldwide, see 14.13.

Pogroms followed the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881, and the May Laws followed in 1882. The Kishinev pogrom of 1903 left '45 dead and hundreds of wounded', and the dead of the 1905 wave were estimated at over 800. 'A mass Jewish emigration began from Russia to the United States.' [[c-us5-immig-pogroms]] The National Park Service calls Manhattan's Lower East Side 'America's iconic immigrant neighborhood'; one tenement, 97 Orchard Street, was home to an estimated 7,000 people from more than 20 nations between 1863 and 1935. [[c-us5-immig-les]] Jewish and Italian immigrant women made up most of the dead in the Triangle fire of 1911 (US5.3). [[c-us5-lab-triangle]] After 1910 revolution in Mexico and a strong American economy drew more Mexicans north, and the census count of Mexican immigrants tripled from 200,000 to 600,000 by 1930. [[c-us5-immig-mexico]]

Did the new immigrants get ahead? Older cross-sectional studies found that immigrants started in lower-paid occupations than natives and then caught up quickly. Following the same individuals in linked records, Ran Abramitzky, Leah Boustan and Katherine Eriksson (2014) found that 'the average immigrant did not face a substantial occupation-based earnings penalty upon first arrival' and moved up at the same pace as natives. The apparent early gap and rapid catch-up reflected the declining quality of later arrival cohorts and the 'departures of negatively-selected return migrants'. [[c-us5-immig-abe]] A 2021 study by Abramitzky, Boustan, Elisa Jácome and Santiago Pérez finds that, then as now, 'children of immigrants from nearly every sending country have higher rates of upward mobility than children of the US-born.' [[c-us5-immig-kids]] Marco Tabellini (2020) finds that immigration in 1910-30 raised natives' employment and output, but also brought more support for restriction, less redistribution and more conservative legislators, and that 'natives' political discontent was increasing in the cultural differences between immigrants and natives.' [[c-us5-immig-tabellini]]

The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 'suspended the immigration of Chinese laborers (skilled or unskilled) for a period of 10 years'; the Geary Act renewed it in 1892, and exclusion was repealed only in 1943. [[c-us5-immig-exclusion]] Recorded immigrants from China (DHS Table 2) fell from 133,139 in the 1870s to 15,268 in the 1890s. [[c-us5-immig-dhs]] The Immigration Act of 1917 'required immigrants over 16 years old to demonstrate basic reading comprehension in any language' and created an 'Asiatic Barred Zone'; it 'passed by an overwhelming majority over the veto of President Woodrow Wilson.' [[c-us5-immig-1917]] Wilson had called the literacy test 'not a test of character, of quality, or of personal fitness' but a 'penalty for lack of opportunity', as he had argued in vetoing a similar bill in 1915. [[c-us5-immig-veto]]

pages.title: Cities and the Gilded Age
pages.lede: Between 1880 and 1920 the share of Americans the census counted as urban rose from 28.2 to 51.2 percent. Jacob Riis photographed New York's slums, Tammany Hall ran the city's Democrats, and Jane Addams opened Hull-House in Chicago. Wealth was highly concentrated early in the 20th century, but whether income inequality rose after 1870 is disputed.
body: Between 1880 and 1920 the population of the United States more than doubled, from 50.2 million to 106.0 million, and the share counted as urban rose from 28.2 percent to 51.2. [[c-us5-city-urban]] 'Urban' was a census definition: from 1910 a place counted if it had at least 2,500 inhabitants, while the censuses of 1880 to 1900 had used minimum sizes of 8,000, 4,000 and 2,500, and 1920 was the first census in which more than half of Americans were counted as urban. [[c-us5-city-def]] The shares given here all come from one series in the Census Bureau's Table 4, under what it calls the 'previous urban definition'. [[c-us5-city-urban]] New York, counted across its five boroughs, grew from 3,437,202 people in 1900 to 5,620,048 in 1920. [[c-us5-city-nyc]] On immigration to the cities, see US5.4.

In How the Other Half Lives (1890) Jacob Riis wrote that in New York 'three-fourths of its people live in the tenements', and that 'more than twelve hundred thousand persons call them home'; these were his own estimates. [[c-us5-city-riis]] He photographed the slums inside and out with a flash lamp, and his book stimulated the first significant New York legislation to curb tenement house evils. [[c-us5-city-riis-photo]]

Tammany Hall, 'the executive committee of the Democratic Party in New York City', had come under the complete domination of William M. Tweed in 1868, and under him the city was plundered of more than $200 million. [[c-us5-city-tammany]] Yet Tammany's district leaders could be counted on to help poor families in distress, and, in Britannica's words, 'The helping hand outweighed all of the denunciations.' [[c-us5-city-tammany-help]] In Chicago, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull-House in 1889; Addams later won the Nobel Peace Prize, in 1931. [[c-us5-city-hullhouse]]

The era's name comes from The Gilded Age (1873), a novel by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner. [[c-us5-city-gilded]] Britannica dates the age itself narrowly, to the 1870s. [[c-us5-city-gilded-dates]] How unequal it was is disputed. Saez and Zucman find wealth highly concentrated at the start of the 20th century, falling from 1929 to 1978 and rising again after 1979. [[c-us5-city-wealth]] Lindert and Williamson date their two great waves of rising income inequality to 1774-1860 and the 1970s onward. [[c-us5-city-lw]] Vincent Geloso takes Lindert and Williamson's estimate for 1870, which he says 'is not disputed', as his starting point, but he and his co-authors argue that Piketty and Saez's figures for 1913 and 1917 'massively overestimate inequality', so that the gap between the top tenth and the rest 'most likely declined' between 1870 and 1910. [[c-us5-city-geloso]]

pages.title: The Populists
pages.lede: Out of the farmers' alliances came the People's Party, whose platform of 4 July 1892 demanded free silver, a graduated income tax and government ownership of the railroads. Its candidate won 8.5 percent of the vote in 1892; in 1896 it nominated the Democrat William Jennings Bryan, who lost to William McKinley. Historians still disagree about what the Populists were.
body: From about 1875 the Farmers' Alliance movement, organized in three large regional groupings, tried to improve farmers' lot through 'the creation of cooperatives and political advocacy'. [[c-us5-pop-alliance]] Out of this cooperative crusade came the People's, or Populist, Party, formally organized in 1892; on 4 July its founding convention adopted the Omaha Platform, whose preamble was written by the Minnesota politician and novelist Ignatius Donnelly. [[c-us5-pop-founding]] Its preamble declared: 'we meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin'. The platform itself declared: 'Wealth belongs to him who creates it, and every dollar taken from industry without an equivalent is robbery.' [[c-us5-pop-preamble]]

The platform demanded the free and unlimited coinage of silver and gold at a ratio of 16 to 1 (on the money question see US5.2); 'We demand a graduated income tax'; that 'the government should own and operate the railroads in the interest of the people'; and that 'postal savings banks be established by the government'. [[c-us5-pop-demands]] Many of its proposals, among them the graduated income tax, the secret ballot, the direct election of senators and the eight-hour day, were later enacted in the Progressive and New Deal eras (US5.11). [[c-us5-pop-enacted]]

In 1892 the Populist James B. Weaver won 1,029,357 votes, 8.5 percent, and 22 electoral votes; Grover Cleveland won the presidency. [[c-us5-pop-1892]] In 1896 the Populists nominated Bryan, the Democratic candidate, and, to keep their own identity, Tom Watson for vice president. [[c-us5-pop-fusion]] McKinley won by 271 electoral votes to 176 and 51.1 percent of the popular vote to 45.8. [[c-us5-pop-1896]] Afterwards, 'For all practical purposes, the Populist Party was dead.' [[c-us5-pop-fusion]] In Georgia the Populists, 'never calling for social equality', had courted Black voters, inviting two Black delegates to their 1892 state convention; Watson later demanded the disfranchisement of Black voters. [[c-us5-pop-race]]

What were the Populists? In the summary of a McGraw-Hill textbook essay, John Hicks (1931) saw them as people responding rationally and progressively to economic hardship. [[c-us5-pop-hicks]] Richard Hofstadter (1955) called the movement 'soft' and 'dark': soft because it rested on a nostalgic, unrealistic myth of the past, and dark because it was shot through with bigotry and ignorance. [[c-us5-pop-hofstadter]] Lawrence Goodwyn (1976) answered that it was a 'cooperative crusade' against the 'coercive potential of the emerging corporate state', built on a 'movement culture'. [[c-us5-pop-goodwyn]] Walter Nugent found that the Kansas Populists were not bigoted, and Norman Pollack saw in Populism a sophisticated, far-sighted and even radical vision of reform. [[c-us5-pop-nugent]] Elizabeth Sanders and Michael Kazin argue that Populism outlived 1896. [[c-us5-pop-legacy]] Charles Postel (2007) argues that the Populists were modernizers, and, in Cameron Blevins's reading of the book, that their racism drew on the scientific racism of their day. [[c-us5-pop-postel]]

pages.title: Jim Crow
pages.lede: Mississippi in 1890 and Louisiana in 1898 wrote new constitutions that drove most Black men from the polls, and in 1896 the Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railway accommodations in Plessy v. Ferguson. By Tuskegee's count, lynching peaked in 1892. Booker T. Washington and W. E. B. Du Bois disagreed over how to respond, and in 1909 the NAACP was founded.
body: After Reconstruction ended (US4.11), two state constitutions show how Black men were driven from politics. When Mississippi wrote a new constitution in 1890, many white Mississippians 'were determined to remove Black Mississippians from politics'; literacy tests 'kept almost all Black voters from the polls', and the poll tax kept many Black and white Mississippians from voting. [[c-us5-jc-ms1890]] Louisiana's constitution of 1898 added a literacy test 'with no standards attached', a property alternative and a grandfather clause. Black registration fell from 130,344 to 12,902, and to 5,320 by 1900; white registration fell too, from 164,088 to 74,133, before climbing back to 125,437. [[c-us5-jc-la1898]] 'The poll tax depressed voting for disadvantaged men of both races.' [[c-us5-jc-polltax]]

Louisiana also required railways to provide 'equal but separate accommodations for the white and colored races'. Plessy, described as 'seven eighths Caucasian', paid for a first-class passage from New Orleans to Covington; on 18 May 1896 the Supreme Court upheld the law by 7 to 1. [[c-us5-jc-plessy]] Justice Brown called it a 'fallacy' to assume that 'the enforced separation of the two races stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority.' [[c-us5-jc-brown]] Justice Harlan dissented: 'Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.' The judgment, he predicted, would 'prove to be quite as pernicious as the decision made by this tribunal in the Dred Scott Case' (US4.3). [[c-us5-jc-harlan]]

Tuskegee Institute recorded 4,743 lynchings from 1882 to 1968, 3,445 of them of Black victims; the worst year was 1892, with 230. [[c-us5-jc-tuskegee]] The Equal Justice Initiative, counting racial terror lynchings from 1877 to 1950, documented 4,075 in twelve Southern states alone in its report of 2017, at least 800 more than earlier counts for those states. [[c-us5-jc-eji]] On 21 May 1892 an editorial in the Memphis Free Speech declared: 'Nobody in this section of the country believes the old thread-bare lie that Negro men rape white women.' Creditors then took possession of the paper's office and sold the outfit. Ida B. Wells reprinted the editorial in Southern Horrors (1892), and wrote that 'a Winchester rifle should have a place of honor in every black home'. [[c-us5-jc-wells]]

In Atlanta on 18 September 1895 Booker T. Washington said: 'Cast down your bucket where you are', and 'In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand'. [[c-us5-jc-washington]] In 1903 Du Bois called this the 'Atlanta Compromise', and charged that it asked Black Americans to give up, for the present, political power, insistence on civil rights and the higher education of their young. 'The problem of the Twentieth Century', he wrote, 'is the problem of the color-line.' [[c-us5-jc-dubois]] Washington's strategy, in the words of Harvard University Press's description of Robert Norrell's biography Up from History (2011), 'has been disparaged since the 1960s'; the book presents him, in the historian W. Fitzhugh Brundage's endorsement, as 'a gifted, creative, and flawed activist'. [[c-us5-jc-norrell]] After a race riot in Springfield, Illinois, in 1908, a call issued on 12 February 1909 led to the founding of the NAACP, whose magazine The Crisis Du Bois edited from 1910. [[c-us5-jc-naacp]] The Great Migration began in the 1910s; between the two World Wars about 2 million Black people left the South. [[c-us5-jc-migration]]

pages.title: The West and Native nations
pages.lede: In 1893 Frederick Jackson Turner read the 1890 census's statement that there was hardly a frontier line left as 'the closing of a great historic movement'. Allotment under the Dawes Act cut Native landholdings from 138 to 48 million acres; at Wounded Knee in 1890 soldiers killed some 150 to 300 Lakota; and in 1903 the Supreme Court held that Congress could abrogate treaties. Interior's final report (July 2024) counted at least 973 deaths of children in the federal boarding-school system; a Washington Post investigation (December 2024) counted at least 3,104 between 1828 and 1970.
body: In Chicago on 12 July 1893 Frederick Jackson Turner quoted the superintendent of the 1890 census: up to 1880 'the country had a frontier of settlement', but now 'there can hardly be said to be a frontier line'. This, Turner said, 'marks the closing of a great historic movement.' [[c-us5-west-frontier]] He built his thesis on 'The existence of an area of free land, its continuous recession', and ended that 'with its going has closed the first period of American history'. [[c-us5-west-turner]] Patricia Nelson Limerick's The Legacy of Conquest (1987) attempted, in Kirkus Reviews' words, 'the displacement of the Frederick Jackson Turner school of "closed frontiers"', and, the reviewer wrote, imputed to Turner motives that were 'nationalistic and ethnocentric'. [[c-us5-west-limerick]]

The Dawes Act of 8 February 1887 provided for allotting reservation lands, 'To each head of a family, one-quarter of a section', less to others, and declared allottees citizens. Its fifth section let the Secretary of the Interior negotiate to buy, with a tribe's consent, the parts of a reservation 'not allotted', to be held for 'actual settlers'. [[c-us5-west-dawes]] The Indian Land Tenure Foundation writes that 'the most productive land was identified as "surplus to Indian needs" and sold off to white settlers or business interests', and that Native holdings fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934, when the Indian Reorganization Act ended allotment. [[c-us5-west-land]] The Medicine Lodge treaty had required the consent of three-fourths of a reservation's adult men to any cession. In Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903) the Supreme Court held that 'The power exists to abrogate the provisions of an Indian treaty', and that Congress had exercised 'Plenary authority over the tribal relations of the Indians' from the beginning. [[c-us5-west-lonewolf]]

In 1890 the Ghost Dance religious movement swept across the Plains. On 29 December the 7th Cavalry killed approximately 150 to 300 Lakota at Wounded Knee, among them the Miniconjou band of Sitanka, known to whites as Big Foot; at least 25 soldiers also died. [[c-us5-west-wk]] For the wars of the 1860s see US4.12.

The federal government also ran boarding schools for Native children. Interior's first report (May 2022) listed 408 federal schools in 37 states or then territories between 1819 and 1969, with burial sites at about 53. [[c-us5-west-doi2022]] Its second (July 2024) listed 417 institutions and found that 'at least 973' children died in the system. [[c-us5-west-doi2024]] In December 2024 a Washington Post investigation, drawing on hundreds of thousands of government documents, counted at least 3,104 deaths between 1828 and 1970, more than three times the federal figure. [[c-us5-west-post]]

pages.title: Religion in the Gilded Age
pages.lede: Walter Rauschenbusch drew a Social Gospel from the Hebrew prophets, Pope Leo XIII rejected socialism but defended workers' unions and a wage a frugal worker could live on, and Reform rabbis at Pittsburgh made it their duty to address 'the contrasts and evils' of society. The Fundamentals defended the Bible as 'the inerrant word of God', and the Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in 1919, brought national Prohibition.
body: Walter Rauschenbusch, a German Baptist pastor in New York from 1886, taught, in Britannica's summary, that 'the Kingdom of God required social as well as individual salvation', and became prominent with Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907). [[c-us5-relig-rausch]] Its first chapter traces Christianity's roots to the Hebrew prophets, who, he wrote, 'brushed sacrificial ritual aside altogether as trifling compared with righteousness', and 'said less about the pure heart for the individual than of just institutions for the nation.' [[c-us5-relig-prophets]] Amos is one such prophet; in Amos 5 God says: 'I hate, I despise your festivals, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies', and 'But let justice roll down like water and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream' (Amos 5:21, 24, NRSVUE). [[c-us5-relig-amos]]

In Rome, Pope Leo XIII addressed the condition of workers in Rerum Novarum (1891). He wrote that 'working men have been surrendered, isolated and helpless, to the hardheartedness of employers'. He held that 'community of goods, must be utterly rejected', but that 'wages ought not to be insufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved wage-earner', and that 'The most important of all are workingmen's unions'. [[c-us5-relig-rerum]] In the United States the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore (1884) asked each parish to support a school, and in Chicago the parish became 'a haven for Catholics in the hostile Protestant America'. [[c-us5-relig-parish]] On Catholic and Jewish immigrants, see US5.4.

In November 1885 Reform rabbis meeting at Pittsburgh declared that of the Mosaic law 'today we accept as binding only its moral laws', set aside the rules on 'diet, priestly purity, and dress', and said: 'We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community', expecting 'neither a return to Palestine, nor a sacrificial worship under the sons of Aaron'. [[c-us5-relig-pitt]] Their eighth plank, 'In full accordance with the spirit of the Mosaic legislation, which strives to regulate the relations between rich and poor', pledged them 'to solve, on the basis of justice and righteousness, the problems presented by the contrasts and evils of the present organization of society.' [[c-us5-relig-pitt8]] The Jewish Theological Seminary, founded in New York in 1886, became the centre of Conservative Judaism. [[c-us5-relig-jts]]

The Fundamentals, twelve volumes of 1910-15 funded by Lyman and Milton Stewart, taught that 'the Bible is the inerrant word of God', and by Biola University's count 3 million copies were in print. [[c-us5-relig-fund]] Temperance drew on the churches: the Woman's Christian Temperance Union was founded in Cleveland in 1874, and the Anti-Saloon League 'drew most of its support from Protestant evangelical churches'. [[c-us5-relig-temperance]] The Eighteenth Amendment, prohibiting intoxicating liquors, passed Congress in December 1917 and was ratified in January 1919. [[c-us5-relig-18th]]

pages.title: Empire
pages.lede: In 1898 the United States went to war with Spain after Congress acknowledged Cuban independence, and the peace gave it Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines; the same year it annexed Hawaii, whose queen had been overthrown in 1893 with the support of the American minister and a contingent of Marines. Holding the Philippines took a further war in which, by the Office of the Historian's estimate, as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians died. Historians still disagree over whether this empire was a break with the American past or a continuation of it.
body: Cuban revolutionaries were fighting for independence from Spanish colonial rule, and American outrage at Spain's brutal tactics won them much sympathy. [[c-us5-emp-cuba]] On 15 February 1898 the USS Maine 'exploded and sank in Havana harbor under mysterious circumstances'. [[c-us5-emp-maine]] In April Congress passed a joint resolution that acknowledged Cuban independence and 'foreswore any intention on the part of the United States to annex Cuba'; Spain declared war, and Congress voted for war on 25 April. On 1 May Commodore George Dewey's Asiatic Squadron defeated the Spanish naval force defending the Philippines at Manila Bay, and a cease-fire was signed on 12 August. [[c-us5-emp-war]] By the Treaty of Paris of 10 December Spain ceded Guam and Puerto Rico and agreed to sell the Philippines to the United States for $20 million. [[c-us5-emp-paris]] The Library of Congress puts the war's cost at $250 million and 3,000 American lives, 90 percent of them lost to infectious disease. [[c-us5-emp-cost]]

The Filipinos had proclaimed a republic of their own. Revolutionaries led by Emilio Aguinaldo had taken most of Luzon, and on 4 February 1899, two days before the Senate ratified the treaty, fighting broke out between them and American forces. The war became a guerrilla struggle that lasted beyond Aguinaldo's capture in 1901 and into the spring of 1902; American forces at times burned villages, imposed civilian reconcentration policies and tortured suspected guerrillas. Theodore Roosevelt declared the war over on 4 July 1902, although uprisings against American rule broke out from time to time in the years that followed. [[c-us5-emp-philwar]] The Office of the Historian counts over 4,200 American and over 20,000 Filipino combatants dead, and estimates that as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians died from violence, famine and disease. [[c-us5-emp-phildeaths]]

Hawaii came by another road. On 17 January 1893 a committee of non-native American businessmen and politicians with sugar interests overthrew Queen Lili'uokalani in a bloodless coup, with support from the U.S. minister to Hawaii and a contingent of Marines, and proclaimed a Provisional Government headed by Sanford Dole. President Cleveland's investigator, James Blount, found that she had been overthrown illegally, but on 7 July 1898 Congress annexed the islands by joint resolution, and in December the queen sent the House of Representatives a memorial protesting the American claim. [[c-us5-emp-hawaii]] In Puerto Rico the Foraker Act of 1900 ended military rule and set up a 'temporary civil government', but did not make Puerto Ricans citizens; the Jones-Shafroth Act of 2 March 1917 did, for those born on or after 25 April 1898. [[c-us5-emp-pr]] When an importer sought to recover the duties he had paid on oranges from San Juan, the Supreme Court held in Downes v. Bidwell (1901), as the case syllabus puts it, that 'The Island of Porto Rico is not a part of the United States' within the constitutional clause requiring duties to be 'uniform throughout the United States'. [[c-us5-emp-downes]] Farther afield, Secretary of State John Hay's Open Door note of 6 September 1899 proposed equal trading opportunity in China for merchants of all nationalities, and in July 1900, during the Boxer Rebellion, he asked the powers to respect China's 'territorial and administrative integrity'. [[c-us5-emp-opendoor]] In 1903, after Colombia's congress rejected the financial terms of a canal treaty, Panama declared independence on 3 November while Roosevelt sent warships to Panama City and Colón; the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty gave the United States a 10-mile-wide strip for $10 million and $250,000 a year, and the canal was completed in 1914. [[c-us5-emp-panama]]

Not everyone approved. The Anti-Imperialist League's platform of 1899 declared: 'We hold that the policy known as imperialism is hostile to liberty and tends toward militarism'. [[c-us5-emp-antiimp]] Historians still argue over what 1898 meant. In Naoko Shibusawa's summary, Samuel Flagg Bemis (1936) saw the colonization of the Philippines as an aberration from American policy and a great mistake, one that overextended the country's budget and armed forces. [[c-us5-emp-bemis]] Charles Beard, from 1914, saw it instead as a continuation of American efforts to extend commercial power, and William Appleman Williams (1964) argued that settling the continent had itself been colonialism, for there was 'no serious justification for making the crossing of water a necessary condition of colonialism'; Naoko Shibusawa notes that this view of continuity 'has become more mainstream during the twenty-first century'. [[c-us5-emp-continuity]] Kristin Hoganson (1998) and Gail Bederman (1995) turned to the mindsets behind the policy, showing, in Shibusawa's phrase, how notions of 'manly honor and civilizational progress' also shaped it. [[c-us5-emp-gender]]

pages.title: The Progressives
pages.lede: Muckraking journalists exposed the hazards of the marketplace, and between 1890 and 1914 Congress outlawed combinations in restraint of trade, banned the interstate transport of unlawful food and drugs and created the Federal Trade Commission, while two amendments of 1913 brought an income tax and the direct election of senators. Theodore Roosevelt protected about 230 million acres of public land, and under Woodrow Wilson members of the cabinet segregated federal departments. Who the Progressives were, and whose interests they served, has divided historians since Richard Hofstadter's The Age of Reform (1955).
body: In a speech of April 1906 Theodore Roosevelt invoked 'the Man with the Muck-rake' from Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, while insisting that 'There should be relentless exposure of and attack upon every evil man whether politician or business man'. [[c-us5-prog-muckrake]] Muckraking journalists such as Samuel Hopkins Adams exposed the hazards of the marketplace in vivid detail, and the condition of the meat-packing industry that Upton Sinclair captured in The Jungle was, in the words of the Food and Drug Administration, 'the final precipitating force behind both a meat inspection law and a comprehensive food and drug law'. On 30 June 1906 Roosevelt signed the Food and Drugs Act, which banned the interstate transport of unlawful food and drugs and required that labels not be false or misleading. [[c-us5-prog-food]] Against the trusts there was already a law. The Sherman Anti-Trust Act of 2 July 1890 outlawed combinations in restraint of interstate and foreign trade, but it was loosely worded, and in 1895 the Supreme Court found that American Sugar had not broken it even though the company controlled about 98 percent of sugar refining. [[c-us5-prog-sherman]] Under Roosevelt the act was used 'with considerable success': in 1904 the Court upheld the government's suit to dissolve the Northern Securities Company, holding, in the words of the reporter's syllabus, that the arrangement was 'an illegal combination in restraint of interstate commerce', and President Taft later used the act against Standard Oil and American Tobacco. [[c-us5-prog-trusts]]

Roosevelt created the present-day Forest Service in 1905, and the Antiquities Act he signed on 8 June 1906 let him proclaim 18 national monuments; in all, the National Park Service credits him with protecting about 230 million acres of public land. [[c-us5-prog-conserv]] Two amendments of 1913 changed how the government was paid for and chosen. The Sixteenth, ratified on 3 February, allowed a tax on incomes (on the doctrine, see US2.13), [[c-us5-prog-16th]] and the Seventeenth, ratified by three-quarters of the states by 8 April, ended the election of senators by state legislatures, several of which had deadlocked over it (US2.1). [[c-us5-prog-17th]] Woodrow Wilson ran on a 'New Freedom' platform that, in the Miller Center's words, 'touted social justice and opportunity for all Americans'. In office he signed the Underwood Tariff, with 'the most significant reductions in rates since the Civil War' and a small graduated income tax, the Federal Reserve Act (US5.2), and the Clayton Act, which excluded labor and farm organizations from prosecution under the Sherman Act. [[c-us5-prog-wilson]] On 26 September 1914 the Federal Trade Commission was created, with power to investigate and publicize unfair and anti-competitive business practices. [[c-us5-prog-ftc]]

Wilson allowed members of his cabinet to introduce segregation into federal departments such as the Post Office and the Treasury, and African Americans protested. [[c-us5-prog-wilsonseg]] Linking newly digitized personnel records for 1907-1921 to the census, the economists Abhay Aneja and Guo Xu estimate that segregation widened the Black-white earnings gap in the civil service by 3.4 to 6.9 percentage points, mainly by moving Black civil servants to lower-paid positions. Its effects outlasted Wilson's presidency: Black civil servants' home ownership fell relative to white civil servants', and their children grew up to have less education, lower earnings and less social mobility. [[c-us5-prog-aneja]] Thomas C. Leonard's Illiberal Reformers (2016) traces the influence of Darwinism, racial science and eugenics on Progressive-era economists and reformers; in its publisher's summary, they proposed using the regulatory state 'not to help those they portrayed as hereditary inferiors, but to exclude them'. Marshall Steinbaum and Bernard Weisberger (2017) granted that early economists held such views but replied that they 'were common to a broad swath of the intellectual elite of that era', including the Progressives' opponents, and that Leonard judges the period anachronistically; Phillip Magness (2018) defended Leonard against them. [[c-us5-prog-leonard]]

Who were the Progressives? Alan Brinkley's survey of the debate sets out the main answers. Richard Hofstadter (1955) explained them by the 'status anxiety' of upper-middle-class families whose prestige was declining, a discontent that, in Brinkley's words, was 'psychological, not economic'. [[c-us5-prog-hofstadter]] Gabriel Kolko (1963) argued that corporate leaders themselves sought federal regulation, to shield their firms from competition. [[c-us5-prog-kolko]] Robert Wiebe (1967) saw a 'new middle class' seeking national institutions to stabilize and enhance its position. [[c-us5-prog-wiebe]] J. Joseph Huthmacher and John Buenker credited immigrant workers and urban machines with much of the reform; Peter Filene (1970) doubted that a single Progressive movement had existed at all; Daniel Rodgers (1998) traced its roots to a global process of change; and Michael McGerr (2003), as Brinkley puts it, portrayed it as 'an essentially moral project'. [[c-us5-prog-others]]

pages.title: Women and the vote
pages.lede: The demand for the vote made at Seneca Falls in 1848 divided the movement in 1869 over the Fifteenth Amendment, and it was first won in the West, where Wyoming Territory enfranchised women in 1869. By 1919, by the Bill of Rights Institute's count, women had full suffrage in 15 states, and it lists 12 more where they could vote for federal offices (in Ohio and Indiana the 1917 laws were soon overturned); in August 1920 the Nineteenth Amendment barred denial of the vote on account of sex. Many women still could not vote because of discriminatory state laws, and Black women in the Jim Crow South met the same disfranchising tactics used against Black men.
body: The Declaration of Sentiments adopted at Seneca Falls in 1848 (US3.4) began from the claim that 'all men and women are created equal' and listed among man's wrongs that 'He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.' [[c-us5-suff-sentiments]] After the Civil War the question was whose vote came first. At the American Equal Rights Association's meeting of 12 May 1869 the movement broke apart over the Fifteenth Amendment, which covered race but not sex. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, for whom any amendment without women's suffrage was unacceptable, founded the National Woman Suffrage Association to seek a constitutional amendment, while Lucy Stone and Julia Ward Howe's American Woman Suffrage Association worked for suffrage laws state by state. Frederick Douglass supported the Fifteenth Amendment, arguing that the ballot was more urgent for Black men than for women. [[c-us5-suff-split]] In that fight Stanton argued that African Americans were ignorant of the country's laws and customs, and said it was 'a serious question whether we had better stand aside and see "Sambo" walk into the kingdom [of civil rights] first.' [[c-us5-suff-stanton]]

The vote was won first in the West. 'The territory of Wyoming granted women the vote in 1869.' [[c-us5-suff-wyoming]] Utah Territory followed in 1870 and Washington Territory in 1883, then the states of Colorado in 1893 and Idaho in 1896, and by 1912, the National Archives notes, nine western states had adopted woman suffrage. [[c-us5-suff-west]] Not every early grant was full or lasting: Washington's territorial supreme court overturned its law in 1887, Congress rescinded the vote of Utah's women the same year, and Montana Territory's grant of 1887 covered school elections only. [[c-us5-suff-lost]] On the Bill of Rights Institute's list, New York in 1917 was the first state east of the Mississippi where women won the vote in state elections. By 1919, the Institute says, they had full suffrage in 15 states, and it lists 12 more where they could vote for federal offices, from Illinois in 1913 to Tennessee in 1919, though Ohio's law of 1917 was repealed by referendum that November and Indiana's struck down by its supreme court that October; [[c-us5-suff-lost]] in the other 21, all in the South or the East except New Mexico, women could be denied the vote until the Nineteenth Amendment. [[c-us5-suff-bystate]]

The movement's divisions over race did not end in 1869. Sharon Harley writes that the mainstream movement 'even condoned white supremacist ideologies in order to garner southern support for white women's voting rights'. Black women organized on their own: the National Association of Colored Women, founded in 1896, elected Mary Church Terrell its first national president. At the 1913 suffrage parade in Washington, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, who had organized the Chicago-based Alpha Suffrage Club that year, 'refused to join her fellow Black suffragists at the rear', while Terrell marched with the all-Black delegation. [[c-us5-suff-harley]] Martha S. Jones's Vanguard (2020) tells how Black women, in its publisher's words, 'defied both racism and sexism to fight for the ballot'. [[c-us5-suff-jones]]

The House passed the Nineteenth Amendment on 21 May 1919 and the Senate two weeks later, and Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify it, on 18 August 1920. It reads: 'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex. Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.' [[c-us5-suff-nineteenth]] Yet, the National Archives notes, 'Many women remained unable to vote long into the 20th century because of discriminatory state voting laws', and Black women in the Jim Crow South 'encountered the very same disfranchisement strategies' used against Black men (US5.7). [[c-us5-suff-after]] Paid work changed more slowly. Claudia Goldin, who received the economics prize in 2023, showed that women's participation in the labor force traced a U-shaped curve over two centuries. At the beginning of the twentieth century, in the prize committee's words, 'While around twenty per cent of all women worked for pay, only five per cent of married women did so', and the records often listed women only as wives, though they worked on family farms and in businesses or produced goods at home. [[c-us5-suff-goldin]]

pages.title: The United States in the First World War
pages.lede: The United States entered the war in April 1917, after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and a decoded German telegram proposed an alliance with Mexico, with Mexico to reconquer territory in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. About 24 million men registered for the draft, and the Espionage Act brought prosecutions for speech that the Supreme Court upheld in Schenck (1919). Influenza killed about 675,000 Americans, the Justice Department raided suspected radicals after the war, and the Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles.
body: The sinking of the British liners Lusitania and Arabic had killed 131 American citizens. On 31 January 1917 the German ambassador, Count Johann von Bernstorff, told Secretary of State Robert Lansing that Germany would restart unrestricted submarine warfare the next day; Wilson still left open the possibility of negotiating with Germany if its submarines refrained from attacking American shipping. [[c-us5-ww1-neutral]] In January British cryptographers had deciphered a telegram from the German foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, to the German ambassador in Mexico City; Britain passed it to Wilson on 24 February, and it was published widely in the American press on 1 March. [[c-us5-ww1-zimmermann]] In the National Archives' transcript it reads: 'We intend to begin on the first of February unrestricted submarine warfare. We shall endeavor in spite of this to keep the United States of America neutral. In the event of this not succeeding, we make Mexico a proposal or [sic] alliance on the following basis: make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The settlement in detail is left to you. You will inform the President of the above most secretly as soon as the outbreak of war with the United States of America is certain and add the suggestion that he should, on his own initiative, invite Japan to immediate adherence and at the same time mediate between Japan and ourselves. Please call the President's attention to the fact that the ruthless employment of our submarines now offers the prospect of compelling England in a few months to make peace. Signed, ZIMMERMANN.' [[c-us5-ww1-zimmtext]]

On 2 April 1917 Wilson asked Congress for war: 'The world must be made safe for democracy.' [[c-us5-ww1-message]] The Senate voted for war by 82 to 6 on 4 April, and the House concurred two days later, by 373 to 50. Jeannette Rankin of Montana, elected in 1916 as the first woman member of Congress, voted no: 'I want to stand by my country, but I cannot vote for war.' [[c-us5-ww1-vote]] Six weeks after the declaration only 73,000 men had enlisted, against a hoped-for army of 1 million volunteers. The Selective Service Act, passed on 18 May 1917, required men aged 21 to 30, and later up to 45, to register, and about 24 million did. The National Archives says that '4.8 million went to war', 2.8 million of them drafted and 2 million volunteers. [[c-us5-ww1-draft]] The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 4,734,991 servicemembers worldwide, with 53,402 battle deaths, 63,114 other deaths in service and 204,002 wounded. [[c-us5-ww1-va]]

The Espionage Act of 15 June 1917 allowed the prosecution of anyone who 'interfered with or attempted to undermine the United States' war effort', with up to 20 years in prison and a $10,000 fine, and the Sedition Act of 1918 made it a crime to 'speak ill of or criticize the American government', the Constitution or the flag; it was repealed three years later. [[c-us5-ww1-espionage]] The defendants in Schenck v. United States were convicted under the Espionage Act for a document that 'intimated that conscription was despotism in its worst form'. On 3 March 1919 Justice Holmes, for a unanimous Court, upheld the convictions: 'The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.' He set out a test: 'The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent.' [[c-us5-ww1-schenck]] (For the standard the Court adopted in 1969, see US2.9.) Eugene V. Debs, a leading Socialist, was indicted under the same act for an anti-war speech at Canton, Ohio, on 16 June 1918; the Supreme Court upheld the verdict in 1919, and he was sentenced to ten years in prison; President Harding commuted the sentence to time served in December 1921. [[c-us5-ww1-debs]]

In the United States the influenza of 1918 was first identified among military personnel that spring, and it killed about 675,000 Americans, out of at least 50 million deaths worldwide (15.1). [[c-us5-ww1-flu]] After the war came bombings and raids. On 2 June 1919 the anarchist Carlo Valdinoci blew up the front of the home of the new Attorney General, A. Mitchell Palmer, one of a series of coordinated attacks that day. A young Justice Department lawyer, J. Edgar Hoover, was put in charge of gathering intelligence; in December radicals including Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman were put on a ship dubbed the 'Red Ark'; and in January 1920 simultaneous raids in major cities called on local police to arrest thousands of suspected anarchists. The operation's constitutionality was questioned, and Palmer and Hoover were roundly criticized. [[c-us5-ww1-palmer]] The peace failed in the Senate. Reservationists led by Henry Cabot Lodge, and Irreconcilables, opposed the Treaty of Versailles, citing Article 10 on collective security and the League of Nations; on 19 March 1920 it 'fell short of ratification by seven votes', and the United States signed a separate Treaty of Berlin on 25 August 1921 (15.3). [[c-us5-ww1-versailles]]
